children: By Dennis Daniel

As artificial intelligence (AI) accelerates demand for computing infrastructure, data centre developers and operators worldwide are grappling with how to design facilities that can meet future requirements for power, cooling, efficiency, and scalability.

Compared with traditional data centre deployments, AI infrastructure must be resilient, resource-efficient, and built for long-term performance, while reflecting the operating realities and constraints of individual markets.

The Middle East has a unique opportunity to shape a new model for AI infrastructure built around the region's own priorities, according to Manish Pant, Executive Vice President, International Operations at Schneider Electric.

“The Middle East can set a new benchmark for AI infrastructure, from grid to chip and chip to chiller. This is not simply about adding data centres. It is about designing for the region’s priorities: resilient power, water efficiency and speed,” Pant said.
Retrofitting or new-build

As operators evaluate their AI strategies, one of the most pressing questions is whether existing facilities can be adapted for AI workloads or whether entirely new infrastructure must be designed from the ground up.
Pant said the AI infrastructure build-out in the Middle East and Africa allows operators to design around the region’s operating realities rather than inherit legacy constraints.

“Retrofitting will remain viable in some cases, but AI materially raises the performance threshold, particularly where high ambient temperatures, water scarcity, and variable grid conditions must shape design decisions from the start,” he said.

He noted that AI is already reshaping data centre engineering requirements - current high-density AI systems could exceed 100 kilowatts (kW) per rack, while future configurations were projected to reach approximately 800 kW.

“That is not a simple upgrade. It changes how power, cooling, and controls must work together. Integrating these systems provides operators with a clearer view of energy, cooling, space, and performance and the flexibility to scale infrastructure as workloads change,” he said.
In a region where climate conditions and water efficiency are critical considerations, Schneider Electric advocates an integrated design approach from the outset.
“Planning these systems together from the start can improve resilience, efficiency, and visibility across operations,” Pant said.
Integrated management

Schneider Electric’s 2026 data centre research emphasises that modern Data Centre Infrastructure Management (DCIM) must move beyond monitoring into a strategic layer that provides vendor-neutral visibility, predictive analytics, digital twins, and real-time insight across multi-vendor environments.

“Interoperability matters because AI-ready infrastructure cannot be treated as a late-stage cooling upgrade. Electrical distribution, thermal design, liquid cooling, controls, serviceability, and cybersecurity must be engineered together and around local operating conditions,” Pant said.

With AI hardware, power densities, and cooling technologies evolving faster than traditional infrastructure planning and design cycles, futureproofing has emerged as a central consideration for operators making long-term infrastructure investments.

He continued: “For hyperscale and colocation operators in the Middle East and Africa, futureproofing means designing infrastructure that can adapt as AI hardware, power densities, and cooling requirements evolve. In practice, this means choosing modular, interoperable architectures that can scale without requiring a major redesign every few years.”
Standardised designs

Pant pointed to digital twins, electrical simulation, Schneider Electric’s Ecostruxure platform, and validated reference designs as mechanisms for modelling energy flows, cooling performance, power quality, and operational risk before the start of construction.

“An example of how we are bringing this to life is through our collaboration with Foxconn. We are co-developing reference architectures for AI data centres, including modular power and cooling infrastructure and standardised design frameworks. The idea is to create repeatable designs that allow customers to deploy AI capacity faster and adapt as compute, power, and cooling requirements evolve,” he said.
For Schneider Electric, building AI-ready data centres is an end-to-end approach spanning design, simulation, construction, commissioning, operations, maintenance, and optimisation.

“Schneider Electric connects every stage of the AI data centre lifecycle through its capabilities in electrical distribution, critical power, cooling, prefabricated modules, digital twins, DCIM, cybersecurity, field services, and sustainability advisory. The result is faster deployment, stronger operational performance, and lower energy use and emissions,” Pant said.
He pointed to a broader opportunity for the Middle East to use AI to improve efficiency across buildings, industry, infrastructure, and transport.
“The Middle East can build a model shaped by its own priorities, bringing together energy, AI and industrial intelligence,” he said.

Schneider Electric’s UAE Industrial AI Study found that 59 percent of manufacturers surveyed expect AI to have a transformational impact by 2030. That compares with 42.2 percent of respondents in the global sample. In Saudi Arabia, the company is working with DataVolt to support sustainable data centre capacity for the Kingdom’s AI growth.

“Our role is to help customers build infrastructure that is resilient, resource-efficient, and designed for local needs. With the right architecture and intelligence, power, cooling, water, and operations can become a competitive advantage,” he said.
(Reporting by Dennis Daniel; Editing by Anoop Menon)
